Real Analysis — 00 · The Real Numbers and Completeness

Created2026-03-07|Updated2026-03-07|Mathematics > Real Analysis
|Post View:

Calculus teaches how to use limits, derivatives and integrals. Real analysis asks why they work at all: what a real number is, what "gets arbitrarily close" means, and which hidden assumption makes the Intermediate Value Theorem or the convergence of ∑1/n2\sum 1/n^2∑1/n2 true. The answer, again and again, is one property of R\mathbb{R}R that the rationals Q\mathbb{Q}Q lack: completeness, the fact that R\mathbb{R}R has no gaps. This course rebuilds single-variable calculus on that one axiom, with proofs. It follows the standard undergraduate route of Abbott's Understanding Analysis, with Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Bartle and Sherbert's Introduction to Real Analysis, Tao's Analysis I and Spivak's Calculus as parallel reading. This first post sets up the language of proof, the axioms of an ordered field, the supremum and the Axiom of Completeness, and its first consequences: the Archimedean property, density of Q\mathbb{Q}Q, the existence of 2\sqrt{2}2​, nested intervals, and the fact that R\mathbb{R}R is uncountable.

Series map: 00 The Real Numbers & Completeness (this post) → 01 Sequences & Series → 02 Topology of ℝ & Continuity → 03 Differentiation & Taylor's Theorem → 04 The Riemann Integral → 05 Uniform Convergence & Power Series.

Learning Outcome

  • Read and write statements with the quantifiers "for all" (∀\forall∀) and "there exists" (∃\exists∃), and negate nested statements such as "for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is a δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 …" correctly.
  • Use the three core proof patterns — direct proof, proof by contradiction, and induction — and prove that 2\sqrt{2}2​ is irrational.
  • List the ordered field axioms and prove the triangle inequality from them.
  • Define upper bound, supremum and infimum, and use the ε\varepsilonε-characterization of the supremum.
  • State the Axiom of Completeness and explain why Q\mathbb{Q}Q fails it.
  • Prove the Archimedean property, the density of Q\mathbb{Q}Q in R\mathbb{R}R, and the existence of 2\sqrt{2}2​ in R\mathbb{R}R.
  • State and prove the Nested Interval Property.
  • Show that Q\mathbb{Q}Q is countable and that R\mathbb{R}R is uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument), and describe the Cantor set.

Chapter 1 — Logic and proof

Analysis is written in a small, precise language. Most mistakes in a first analysis course are not mistakes about numbers; they are mistakes about quantifiers.

Terminology

  • Statement — a sentence that is either true or false, e.g. "777 is prime".
  • Implication "P⇒QP \Rightarrow QP⇒Q" — "if PPP then QQQ". It is false only when PPP is true and QQQ is false.
  • Converse of P⇒QP \Rightarrow QP⇒Q — the statement Q⇒PQ \Rightarrow PQ⇒P. It is a different statement and may be false.
  • Contrapositive of P⇒QP \Rightarrow QP⇒Q — the statement ¬Q⇒¬P\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P¬Q⇒¬P. It is logically equivalent to the original.
  • Universal quantifier ∀\forall∀ — "for all". Existential quantifier ∃\exists∃ — "there exists (at least one)".
  • Counterexample — one specific object that shows a "for all" statement is false.

Negating quantified statements

The two rules are:

¬(∀x, P(x))  ⟺  ∃x, ¬P(x),¬(∃x, P(x))  ⟺  ∀x, ¬P(x).\neg\big(\forall x,\ P(x)\big) \iff \exists x,\ \neg P(x), \qquad \neg\big(\exists x,\ P(x)\big) \iff \forall x,\ \neg P(x). ¬(∀x, P(x))⟺∃x, ¬P(x),¬(∃x, P(x))⟺∀x, ¬P(x).

To negate a nested statement, move the ¬\neg¬ from left to right, flipping every quantifier it passes, and negate the final condition. The definition of "the sequence (an)(a_n)(an​) converges to aaa" (see Real Analysis 01) is

∀ε>0  ∃N∈N  ∀n≥N:  ∣an−a∣<ε.\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \ \exists N \in \mathbb{N}\ \ \forall n \ge N:\ \ \lvert a_n - a \rvert < \varepsilon. ∀ε>0  ∃N∈N  ∀n≥N:  ∣an​−a∣<ε.

Its negation, "(an)(a_n)(an​) does not converge to aaa", is

∃ε>0  ∀N∈N  ∃n≥N:  ∣an−a∣≥ε.\exists \varepsilon > 0\ \ \forall N \in \mathbb{N}\ \ \exists n \ge N:\ \ \lvert a_n - a \rvert \ge \varepsilon. ∃ε>0  ∀N∈N  ∃n≥N:  ∣an​−a∣≥ε.

In words: there is one fixed tolerance ε\varepsilonε such that, however far out you go, some later term is still at least ε\varepsilonε away from aaa.

The same mechanical rule applies to continuity (see Real Analysis 02). "fff is continuous at ccc" is ∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 ∀x: ∣x−c∣<δ⇒∣f(x)−f(c)∣<ε\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists \delta > 0\ \forall x:\ \lvert x - c\rvert < \delta \Rightarrow \lvert f(x) - f(c)\rvert < \varepsilon∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 ∀x: ∣x−c∣<δ⇒∣f(x)−f(c)∣<ε. Its negation is

∃ε>0  ∀δ>0  ∃x:  ∣x−c∣<δ  and  ∣f(x)−f(c)∣≥ε.\exists \varepsilon > 0\ \ \forall \delta > 0\ \ \exists x:\ \ \lvert x - c \rvert < \delta \ \text{ and } \ \lvert f(x) - f(c) \rvert \ge \varepsilon. ∃ε>0  ∀δ>0  ∃x:  ∣x−c∣<δ  and  ∣f(x)−f(c)∣≥ε.

Note that the negation of an implication A⇒BA \Rightarrow BA⇒B is "AAA and not BBB", not another implication.

Watch out: the order of quantifiers matters. "∀x ∃y: y>x\forall x\ \exists y:\ y > x∀x ∃y: y>x" (every real number has a larger one) is true in R\mathbb{R}R. "∃y ∀x: y>x\exists y\ \forall x:\ y > x∃y ∀x: y>x" (one number is larger than all of them) is false. Swapping ∀\forall∀ and ∃\exists∃ changes the meaning completely. In analysis the classic example is uniform continuity (Real Analysis 02), which differs from continuity only by the position of one quantifier.

Three proof patterns

Direct proof. Assume the hypothesis, reach the conclusion by valid steps. Example: if mmm and nnn are even, m+nm + nm+n is even. Write m=2am = 2am=2a, n=2bn = 2bn=2b; then m+n=2(a+b)m + n = 2(a + b)m+n=2(a+b).

Contrapositive and contradiction. To prove P⇒QP \Rightarrow QP⇒Q you may prove ¬Q⇒¬P\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P¬Q⇒¬P instead. In a proof by contradiction you assume the statement is false and derive something impossible. Example: if n2n^2n2 is even, then nnn is even. Contrapositive: if nnn is odd, n=2k+1n = 2k + 1n=2k+1, then n2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1n2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1 is odd.

Induction. To prove P(n)P(n)P(n) for all n∈N={1,2,3,… }n \in \mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}n∈N={1,2,3,…}, prove the base case P(1)P(1)P(1) and the inductive step P(n)⇒P(n+1)P(n) \Rightarrow P(n+1)P(n)⇒P(n+1). This works because of the well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of N\mathbb{N}N has a least element (if PPP failed somewhere, look at the least failure).

Example (Bernoulli's inequality). For every x≥−1x \ge -1x≥−1 and every n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N, (1+x)n≥1+nx(1 + x)^n \ge 1 + nx(1+x)n≥1+nx.

Proof. For n=1n = 1n=1 both sides equal 1+x1 + x1+x. Suppose (1+x)n≥1+nx(1+x)^n \ge 1 + nx(1+x)n≥1+nx. Since 1+x≥01 + x \ge 01+x≥0, multiplying both sides by 1+x1 + x1+x keeps the inequality:

(1+x)n+1≥(1+nx)(1+x)=1+(n+1)x+nx2≥1+(n+1)x,(1+x)^{n+1} \ge (1 + nx)(1 + x) = 1 + (n+1)x + nx^2 \ge 1 + (n+1)x, (1+x)n+1≥(1+nx)(1+x)=1+(n+1)x+nx2≥1+(n+1)x,

because nx2≥0nx^2 \ge 0nx2≥0. ■\blacksquare■

The hypothesis x≥−1x \ge -1x≥−1 is used exactly once, to multiply an inequality by a non-negative number. Bernoulli's inequality is the standard tool for showing rn→0r^n \to 0rn→0 when ∣r∣<1\lvert r \rvert < 1∣r∣<1 (Real Analysis 01).

The square root of 2 is irrational

Theorem. There is no rational number rrr with r2=2r^2 = 2r2=2.

Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that r=p/qr = p/qr=p/q with integers p,qp, qp,q, q≠0q \ne 0q=0, and r2=2r^2 = 2r2=2. Cancel common factors, so that ppp and qqq are not both even. Then p2=2q2p^2 = 2q^2p2=2q2, so p2p^2p2 is even, and by the contrapositive example above ppp is even: p=2kp = 2kp=2k. Substituting, 4k2=2q24k^2 = 2q^24k2=2q2, so q2=2k2q^2 = 2k^2q2=2k2 is even, and qqq is even. Now ppp and qqq are both even, contradicting the choice of p/qp/qp/q in lowest terms. ■\blacksquare■

This is the first sign that Q\mathbb{Q}Q has gaps: the rationals whose square is less than 222 creep up towards a point that is not there.

Chapter 2 — Ordered fields and absolute value

Terminology

  • Field — a set FFF with two operations +++ and ⋅\cdot⋅ satisfying the field axioms below.
  • Ordered field — a field with a relation <<< satisfying the order axioms below.
  • Absolute value — ∣x∣=x\lvert x \rvert = x∣x∣=x if x≥0x \ge 0x≥0 and ∣x∣=−x\lvert x \rvert = -x∣x∣=−x if x<0x < 0x<0.
  • Distance between xxx and yyy — the number ∣x−y∣\lvert x - y \rvert∣x−y∣.

The axioms

A field satisfies, for all x,y,zx, y, zx,y,z:

Axiom Addition Multiplication
Closure x+y∈Fx + y \in Fx+y∈F xy∈Fxy \in Fxy∈F
Associative (x+y)+z=x+(y+z)(x+y)+z = x+(y+z)(x+y)+z=x+(y+z) (xy)z=x(yz)(xy)z = x(yz)(xy)z=x(yz)
Commutative x+y=y+xx + y = y + xx+y=y+x xy=yxxy = yxxy=yx
Identity x+0=xx + 0 = xx+0=x 1⋅x=x1 \cdot x = x1⋅x=x, with 1≠01 \ne 01=0
Inverse some −x-x−x has x+(−x)=0x + (-x) = 0x+(−x)=0 if x≠0x \ne 0x=0, some x−1x^{-1}x−1 has xx−1=1x x^{-1} = 1xx−1=1
Distributive x(y+z)=xy+xzx(y+z) = xy + xzx(y+z)=xy+xz (links the two operations)

An ordered field also has a relation <<< such that:

  1. Trichotomy: for all x,yx, yx,y exactly one of x<yx < yx<y, x=yx = yx=y, y<xy < xy<x holds.
  2. Transitivity: x<yx < yx<y and y<zy < zy<z imply x<zx < zx<z.
  3. Addition: x<yx < yx<y implies x+z<y+zx + z < y + zx+z<y+z.
  4. Multiplication: x<yx < yx<y and 0<z0 < z0<z imply xz<yzxz < yzxz<yz.

Everything in high-school algebra follows. For example, x2≥0x^2 \ge 0x2≥0 for all xxx, and 0<10 < 10<1 (since 1=121 = 1^21=12 and 1≠01 \ne 01=0). If x<yx < yx<y and z<0z < 0z<0 then yz<xzyz < xzyz<xz: multiplying by a negative number flips an inequality.

Both Q\mathbb{Q}Q and R\mathbb{R}R are ordered fields. So these axioms cannot be what distinguishes them; Chapter 3 adds the one axiom that does.

The triangle inequality

Three facts about absolute value, all checked by cases on the signs: ∣xy∣=∣x∣∣y∣\lvert xy \rvert = \lvert x \rvert \lvert y \rvert∣xy∣=∣x∣∣y∣; −∣x∣≤x≤∣x∣-\lvert x \rvert \le x \le \lvert x \rvert−∣x∣≤x≤∣x∣; and for a≥0a \ge 0a≥0, ∣x∣≤a  ⟺  −a≤x≤a\lvert x \rvert \le a \iff -a \le x \le a∣x∣≤a⟺−a≤x≤a.

Theorem (triangle inequality). For all real x,yx, yx,y: ∣x+y∣≤∣x∣+∣y∣\lvert x + y \rvert \le \lvert x \rvert + \lvert y \rvert∣x+y∣≤∣x∣+∣y∣.

Proof. Add −∣x∣≤x≤∣x∣-\lvert x \rvert \le x \le \lvert x \rvert−∣x∣≤x≤∣x∣ and −∣y∣≤y≤∣y∣-\lvert y \rvert \le y \le \lvert y \rvert−∣y∣≤y≤∣y∣:

−(∣x∣+∣y∣)≤x+y≤∣x∣+∣y∣.-(\lvert x \rvert + \lvert y \rvert) \le x + y \le \lvert x \rvert + \lvert y \rvert. −(∣x∣+∣y∣)≤x+y≤∣x∣+∣y∣.

By the third fact with a=∣x∣+∣y∣a = \lvert x \rvert + \lvert y \rverta=∣x∣+∣y∣, this says ∣x+y∣≤∣x∣+∣y∣\lvert x + y \rvert \le \lvert x \rvert + \lvert y \rvert∣x+y∣≤∣x∣+∣y∣. ■\blacksquare■

Two forms are used constantly:

  • Distance form: ∣a−b∣≤∣a−c∣+∣c−b∣\lvert a - b \rvert \le \lvert a - c \rvert + \lvert c - b \rvert∣a−b∣≤∣a−c∣+∣c−b∣ (put x=a−cx = a - cx=a−c, y=c−by = c - by=c−b). Going from aaa to bbb via ccc is never shorter.
  • Reverse triangle inequality: ∣∣x∣−∣y∣∣≤∣x−y∣\big\lvert \lvert x \rvert - \lvert y \rvert \big\rvert \le \lvert x - y \rvert​∣x∣−∣y∣​≤∣x−y∣. (From ∣x∣=∣(x−y)+y∣≤∣x−y∣+∣y∣\lvert x \rvert = \lvert (x - y) + y \rvert \le \lvert x - y \rvert + \lvert y \rvert∣x∣=∣(x−y)+y∣≤∣x−y∣+∣y∣, and the same with xxx and yyy swapped.)

Trick: almost every ε\varepsilonε proof in this course is "add and subtract a middle term, then use the triangle inequality". When you see ∣anbn−ab∣\lvert a_n b_n - ab \rvert∣an​bn​−ab∣, write it as ∣anbn−anb+anb−ab∣\lvert a_n b_n - a_n b + a_n b - ab \rvert∣an​bn​−an​b+an​b−ab∣ and split.

Proving that two numbers are equal

Lemma. Two real numbers aaa and bbb are equal if and only if for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, ∣a−b∣<ε\lvert a - b \rvert < \varepsilon∣a−b∣<ε.

Proof. If a=ba = ba=b then ∣a−b∣=0<ε\lvert a - b \rvert = 0 < \varepsilon∣a−b∣=0<ε. Conversely, suppose a≠ba \ne ba=b. Then ε0=∣a−b∣>0\varepsilon_0 = \lvert a - b \rvert > 0ε0​=∣a−b∣>0, and ∣a−b∣<ε0\lvert a - b \rvert < \varepsilon_0∣a−b∣<ε0​ is false. ■\blacksquare■

This is how analysis proves equalities: not by computing both sides, but by showing their distance is smaller than any positive tolerance.

Chapter 3 — Supremum, infimum and completeness

Terminology

  • Upper bound — bbb is an upper bound of A⊆RA \subseteq \mathbb{R}A⊆R if a≤ba \le ba≤b for every a∈Aa \in Aa∈A. AAA is bounded above if it has one.
  • Lower bound, bounded below — the same with ≥\ge≥. Bounded means bounded above and below.
  • Supremum (least upper bound) — s=sup⁡As = \sup As=supA if (i) sss is an upper bound of AAA, and (ii) s≤bs \le bs≤b for every upper bound bbb of AAA.
  • Infimum (greatest lower bound) — inf⁡A\inf AinfA, defined the same way with the inequalities reversed.
  • Maximum — an element of AAA that is an upper bound of AAA. A set may have a supremum but no maximum.

A supremum is unique when it exists: if s1s_1s1​ and s2s_2s2​ are both least upper bounds, then s1≤s2s_1 \le s_2s1​≤s2​ and s2≤s1s_2 \le s_1s2​≤s1​.

(0,1)(0, 1)(0,1) 111 no 000

{1/n:n∈N}\{1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}{1/n:n∈N} 111 yes 000 (not a min)
N\mathbb{N}N none (not bounded above) — 111

For A={1−1/n}A = \{1 - 1/n\}A={1−1/n}: 111 is an upper bound since 1/n>01/n > 01/n>0. If b<1b < 1b<1, the Archimedean property (Chapter 4) gives nnn with 1/n<1−b1/n < 1 - b1/n<1−b, so 1−1/n>b1 - 1/n > b1−1/n>b and bbb is not an upper bound. Hence sup⁡A=1\sup A = 1supA=1, and 1∉A1 \notin A1∈/A.

The epsilon characterization

Lemma. Let sss be an upper bound of AAA. Then s=sup⁡As = \sup As=supA if and only if for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is some a∈Aa \in Aa∈A with s−ε<as - \varepsilon < as−ε<a.

Proof. (⇒\Rightarrow⇒) Let ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0. Since s−ε<ss - \varepsilon < ss−ε<s and sss is the least upper bound, s−εs - \varepsilons−ε is not an upper bound. So some a∈Aa \in Aa∈A has a>s−εa > s - \varepsilona>s−ε.

(⇐\Leftarrow⇐) Let bbb be any upper bound with b<sb < sb<s. Put ε=s−b>0\varepsilon = s - b > 0ε=s−b>0. By hypothesis some a∈Aa \in Aa∈A has a>s−ε=ba > s - \varepsilon = ba>s−ε=b, contradicting that bbb is an upper bound. So every upper bound bbb satisfies b≥sb \ge sb≥s, and s=sup⁡As = \sup As=supA. ■\blacksquare■

In pictures: nothing in AAA lies to the right of sss, but every window (s−ε,s](s - \varepsilon, s](s−ε,s], however narrow, contains a point of AAA.

The Axiom of Completeness

Axiom of Completeness (least upper bound property). Every nonempty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a supremum in R\mathbb{R}R.

R\mathbb{R}R is defined to be an ordered field that satisfies this axiom. (Such a field exists and is unique up to an order-preserving isomorphism; the standard constructions use Dedekind cuts, as in Rudin Chapter 1, or Cauchy sequences of rationals, as in Tao Chapter 5. This course takes the axiom as the starting point, as Abbott does.)

The axiom for infima follows. If AAA is nonempty and bounded below, then −A={−a:a∈A}-A = \{-a : a \in A\}−A={−a:a∈A} is nonempty and bounded above, and inf⁡A=−sup⁡(−A)\inf A = -\sup(-A)infA=−sup(−A).

Why Q\mathbb{Q}Q fails the axiom. Let S={r∈Q:r2<2}S = \{r \in \mathbb{Q} : r^2 < 2\}S={r∈Q:r2<2}. It is nonempty (1∈S1 \in S1∈S) and bounded above by 222. Suppose it had a least upper bound sss in Q\mathbb{Q}Q. The argument in Chapter 4 (existence of 2\sqrt{2}2​) shows that s2<2s^2 < 2s2<2 and s2>2s^2 > 2s2>2 are both impossible, so s2=2s^2 = 2s2=2; but no rational squares to 222. So SSS has no supremum in Q\mathbb{Q}Q: the rationals have a hole exactly where 2\sqrt{2}2​ should be. Concretely, 1,1.4,1.41,1.414,…1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, \ldots1,1.4,1.41,1.414,… are in SSS (their squares are below 222; for example 1.4142=1.9993961.414^2 = 1.9993961.4142=1.999396), while 1.5,1.42,1.415,…1.5, 1.42, 1.415, \ldots1.5,1.42,1.415,… are rational upper bounds (1.4152=2.0022251.415^2 = 2.0022251.4152=2.002225). Every rational upper bound can be improved, and the two lists close in on a point that Q\mathbb{Q}Q does not contain.

Working with suprema

Two small results, each proved with the lemma above, are used often.

  • Shift: for c∈Rc \in \mathbb{R}c∈R, sup⁡(A+c)=sup⁡A+c\sup(A + c) = \sup A + csup(A+c)=supA+c, where A+c={a+c:a∈A}A + c = \{a + c : a \in A\}A+c={a+c:a∈A}. (If s=sup⁡As = \sup As=supA, then s+cs + cs+c is an upper bound of A+cA + cA+c, and for each ε\varepsilonε some a>s−εa > s - \varepsilona>s−ε gives a+c>(s+c)−εa + c > (s + c) - \varepsilona+c>(s+c)−ε.)
  • Order: if A⊆BA \subseteq BA⊆B, AAA is nonempty and BBB is bounded above, then sup⁡A≤sup⁡B\sup A \le \sup BsupA≤supB. (Every upper bound of BBB is an upper bound of AAA.)

Common pitfall: assuming sup⁡A∈A\sup A \in AsupA∈A. The supremum of (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) is 111, which is not in the set. Proofs that pick "the largest element of AAA" are wrong unless AAA is finite or known to have a maximum.

Chapter 4 — First consequences of completeness

The Archimedean property

Theorem (Archimedean property).
(i) For every x∈Rx \in \mathbb{R}x∈R there is n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N with n>xn > xn>x.
(ii) For every y>0y > 0y>0 there is n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N with 1/n<y1/n < y1/n<y.

Proof. (i) Suppose not: then xxx is an upper bound of N\mathbb{N}N, so by completeness α=sup⁡N\alpha = \sup \mathbb{N}α=supN exists. Then α−1\alpha - 1α−1 is not an upper bound, so some n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N has n>α−1n > \alpha - 1n>α−1. But then n+1>αn + 1 > \alphan+1>α and n+1∈Nn + 1 \in \mathbb{N}n+1∈N, contradicting that α\alphaα is an upper bound of N\mathbb{N}N.
(ii) Apply (i) to x=1/yx = 1/yx=1/y: some n>1/yn > 1/yn>1/y, so 1/n<y1/n < y1/n<y. ■\blacksquare■

This property looks obvious, yet the proof needs completeness: there are ordered fields (for example suitably ordered fields of rational functions) with "infinitely large" elements, where it fails.

Density of the rationals

Theorem (density of Q\mathbb{Q}Q). For all real a<ba < ba<b there is a rational rrr with a<r<ba < r < ba<r<b.

Proof. By the Archimedean property choose n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N with 1/n<b−a1/n < b - a1/n<b−a. Let mmm be the least integer with m>nam > nam>na (it exists by the Archimedean property and well-ordering), so m−1≤na<mm - 1 \le na < mm−1≤na<m. Then a<m/na < m/na<m/n, and

m≤na+1<na+n(b−a)=nb,m \le na + 1 < na + n(b - a) = nb, m≤na+1<na+n(b−a)=nb,

using 1<n(b−a)1 < n(b - a)1<n(b−a). So a<m/n<ba < m/n < ba<m/n<b. ■\blacksquare■

The idea: steps of size 1/n1/n1/n are shorter than the interval, so one of the points m/nm/nm/n must land inside.

Corollary. The irrationals are dense too: between any a<ba < ba<b there is an irrational number. (Find a rational r≠0r \ne 0r=0 with a/2<r<b/2a/\sqrt{2} < r < b/\sqrt{2}a/2​<r<b/2​; then r2r\sqrt{2}r2​ is irrational and lies in (a,b)(a, b)(a,b).)

Existence of the square root of 2

Theorem. There is α∈R\alpha \in \mathbb{R}α∈R with α2=2\alpha^2 = 2α2=2.

Proof sketch. Let T={t∈R:t2<2}T = \{t \in \mathbb{R} : t^2 < 2\}T={t∈R:t2<2}. It is nonempty (1∈T1 \in T1∈T) and bounded above by 222 (if t>2t > 2t>2 then t2>4t^2 > 4t2>4). Let α=sup⁡T\alpha = \sup Tα=supT; note α≥1\alpha \ge 1α≥1. Show that the other two cases of trichotomy are impossible.

Case α2<2\alpha^2 < 2α2<2. For n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N,

(α+1n)2=α2+2αn+1n2≤α2+2α+1n.\left(\alpha + \tfrac{1}{n}\right)^2 = \alpha^2 + \frac{2\alpha}{n} + \frac{1}{n^2} \le \alpha^2 + \frac{2\alpha + 1}{n}. (α+n1​)2=α2+n2α​+n21​≤α2+n2α+1​.

Choose nnn with 1n<2−α22α+1\frac{1}{n} < \frac{2 - \alpha^2}{2\alpha + 1}n1​<2α+12−α2​ (Archimedean property). Then (α+1/n)2<2(\alpha + 1/n)^2 < 2(α+1/n)2<2, so α+1/n∈T\alpha + 1/n \in Tα+1/n∈T, contradicting that α\alphaα is an upper bound.

Case α2>2\alpha^2 > 2α2>2. Now (α−1n)2>α2−2αn\left(\alpha - \tfrac{1}{n}\right)^2 > \alpha^2 - \frac{2\alpha}{n}(α−n1​)2>α2−n2α​. Choose nnn with 1n<α2−22α\frac{1}{n} < \frac{\alpha^2 - 2}{2\alpha}n1​<2αα2−2​; then (α−1/n)2>2(\alpha - 1/n)^2 > 2(α−1/n)2>2, and α−1/n>0\alpha - 1/n > 0α−1/n>0. Any t∈Tt \in Tt∈T with t>α−1/n>0t > \alpha - 1/n > 0t>α−1/n>0 would have t2>(α−1/n)2>2t^2 > (\alpha - 1/n)^2 > 2t2>(α−1/n)2>2, which is impossible. So α−1/n\alpha - 1/nα−1/n is an upper bound of TTT smaller than α\alphaα — a contradiction.

So α2=2\alpha^2 = 2α2=2. ■\blacksquare■

The same argument, with Q\mathbb{Q}Q in place of R\mathbb{R}R, is the proof that {r∈Q:r2<2}\{r \in \mathbb{Q} : r^2 < 2\}{r∈Q:r2<2} has no supremum in Q\mathbb{Q}Q: its supremum would have to square to 222. With more algebra it gives nnn-th roots of every positive real.

The Nested Interval Property

Theorem (Nested Interval Property). For each n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N let In=[an,bn]I_n = [a_n, b_n]In​=[an​,bn​] be a closed bounded interval, with I1⊇I2⊇I3⊇⋯I_1 \supseteq I_2 \supseteq I_3 \supseteq \cdotsI1​⊇I2​⊇I3​⊇⋯. Then ⋂n=1∞In≠∅\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n \ne \emptyset⋂n=1∞​In​=∅.

Proof. Nesting means a1≤a2≤⋯a_1 \le a_2 \le \cdotsa1​≤a2​≤⋯ and ⋯≤b2≤b1\cdots \le b_2 \le b_1⋯≤b2​≤b1​, and an≤bma_n \le b_man​≤bm​ for all n,mn, mn,m (with k=max⁡(n,m)k = \max(n,m)k=max(n,m): an≤ak≤bk≤bma_n \le a_k \le b_k \le b_man​≤ak​≤bk​≤bm​). So the set A={an:n∈N}A = \{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}A={an​:n∈N} is nonempty and bounded above by every bmb_mbm​. Let x=sup⁡Ax = \sup Ax=supA. Then an≤xa_n \le xan​≤x for all nnn (upper bound) and x≤bmx \le b_mx≤bm​ for all mmm (each bmb_mbm​ is an upper bound and xxx is the least). So x∈Inx \in I_nx∈In​ for every nnn. ■\blacksquare■

If in addition the lengths bn−anb_n - a_nbn​−an​ shrink to 000, the intersection is exactly one point.

Watch out: both hypotheses are needed. The open intervals (0,1/n)(0, 1/n)(0,1/n) are nested but their intersection is empty (any x>0x > 0x>0 is excluded once 1/n<x1/n < x1/n<x). The closed but unbounded intervals [n,∞)[n, \infty)[n,∞) are nested with empty intersection too. And in Q\mathbb{Q}Q the property fails: intervals of rationals closing in on 2\sqrt{2}2​ have no common rational point.

Together with the Archimedean property, the Nested Interval Property is equivalent to the Axiom of Completeness. It is the version used in bisection arguments (Bolzano–Weierstrass in Real Analysis 01, the Intermediate Value Theorem in Real Analysis 02).

Chapter 5 — Countable and uncountable sets

Completeness makes R\mathbb{R}R enormously larger than Q\mathbb{Q}Q, even though both are dense. Cardinality makes "larger" precise.

Terminology

  • Function f:A→Bf : A \to Bf:A→B — a rule assigning to each a∈Aa \in Aa∈A one element f(a)∈Bf(a) \in Bf(a)∈B.
  • One-to-one (injective) — f(a1)=f(a2)f(a_1) = f(a_2)f(a1​)=f(a2​) implies a1=a2a_1 = a_2a1​=a2​.
  • Onto (surjective) — every b∈Bb \in Bb∈B equals f(a)f(a)f(a) for some aaa.
  • Bijection — one-to-one and onto. AAA and BBB have the same cardinality, written A∼BA \sim BA∼B, if a bijection A→BA \to BA→B exists.
  • Countable — A∼NA \sim \mathbb{N}A∼N (an infinite list a1,a2,a3,…a_1, a_2, a_3, \dotsa1​,a2​,a3​,… with every element appearing exactly once). Uncountable — infinite and not countable.

The rationals are countable

First, Z\mathbb{Z}Z is countable: the list 0,1,−1,2,−2,3,−3,…0, 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3, \dots0,1,−1,2,−2,3,−3,… is the bijection f:N→Zf : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}f:N→Z with f(n)=(n−1)/2f(n) = (n-1)/2f(n)=(n−1)/2 for odd nnn and f(n)=−n/2f(n) = -n/2f(n)=−n/2 for even nnn.

Theorem. Q\mathbb{Q}Q is countable.

Proof. For each n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N let AnA_nAn​ be the set of rationals that can be written as ±p/q\pm p/q±p/q in lowest terms with integers p≥0p \ge 0p≥0, q≥1q \ge 1q≥1 and p+q=np + q = np+q=n. For example A1={0}A_1 = \{0\}A1​={0}, A2={1,−1}A_2 = \{1, -1\}A2​={1,−1}, A3={1/2,−1/2,2,−2}A_3 = \{1/2, -1/2, 2, -2\}A3​={1/2,−1/2,2,−2}. Each AnA_nAn​ is finite, the AnA_nAn​ are disjoint, and every rational lies in exactly one of them. List A1A_1A1​, then A2A_2A2​, then A3A_3A3​, and so on. This list contains every rational exactly once, so it is a bijection with N\mathbb{N}N. ■\blacksquare■

The reals are uncountable

Theorem (Cantor, 1874; diagonal argument 1891). The interval (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1), and hence R\mathbb{R}R, is uncountable.

Proof. Every x∈(0,1)x \in (0,1)x∈(0,1) has a decimal expansion x=0.d1d2d3…x = 0.d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldotsx=0.d1​d2​d3​…. It is unique if expansions ending in an infinite string of 999s are excluded (so 0.4999…0.4999\ldots0.4999… is written 0.5000…0.5000\ldots0.5000…). Suppose f:N→(0,1)f : \mathbb{N} \to (0,1)f:N→(0,1) were onto, and write

f(1)=0. a11 a12 a13 a14…f(2)=0. a21 a22 a23 a24…f(3)=0. a31 a32 a33 a34…  ⋮\begin{aligned} f(1) &= 0.\,a_{11}\, a_{12}\, a_{13}\, a_{14} \ldots \\ f(2) &= 0.\,a_{21}\, a_{22}\, a_{23}\, a_{24} \ldots \\ f(3) &= 0.\,a_{31}\, a_{32}\, a_{33}\, a_{34} \ldots \\ &\ \ \vdots \end{aligned} f(1)f(2)f(3)​=0.a11​a12​a13​a14​…=0.a21​a22​a23​a24​…=0.a31​a32​a33​a34​…  ⋮​

Define x=0.b1b2b3…x = 0.b_1 b_2 b_3 \ldotsx=0.b1​b2​b3​… by bn=2b_n = 2bn​=2 if ann≠2a_{nn} \ne 2ann​=2 and bn=3b_n = 3bn​=3 if ann=2a_{nn} = 2ann​=2. This xxx lies in (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), its expansion has no 999s (so it is the unique allowed one), and it differs from f(n)f(n)f(n) in the nnn-th digit for every nnn. So x≠f(n)x \ne f(n)x=f(n) for all nnn, and fff is not onto. ■\blacksquare■

Since (0,1)∼R(0,1) \sim \mathbb{R}(0,1)∼R (for example via x↦tan⁡(πx−π/2)x \mapsto \tan(\pi x - \pi/2)x↦tan(πx−π/2)), R\mathbb{R}R is uncountable. Consequences:

  • The irrationals R∖Q\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}R∖Q are uncountable (if they were countable, R\mathbb{R}R would be a union of two countable sets, which is countable).
  • Almost all real numbers are irrational, even though the rationals are dense. Density is about where points are; cardinality is about how many.

Common pitfall: "the diagonal number might equal some f(n)f(n)f(n) with a different expansion". That is exactly why the proof uses the digits 222 and 333 only and excludes trailing 999s: the number xxx has only one decimal expansion, so differing in a digit really means being a different number.

The Cantor set

Start with C0=[0,1]C_0 = [0,1]C0​=[0,1]. Remove the open middle third to get C1=[0,13]∪[23,1]C_1 = [0, \tfrac13] \cup [\tfrac23, 1]C1​=[0,31​]∪[32​,1]. Remove the open middle third of each piece to get C2C_2C2​, a union of 444 intervals of length 19\tfrac1991​. In general CnC_nCn​ is a union of 2n2^n2n closed intervals of length 3−n3^{-n}3−n. The Cantor set is C=⋂n=0∞CnC = \bigcap_{n=0}^\infty C_nC=⋂n=0∞​Cn​.

  • Length removed: at step kkk you remove 2k−12^{k-1}2k−1 intervals of length 3−k3^{-k}3−k, so the total is ∑k=1∞2k−1/3k=1\sum_{k=1}^\infty 2^{k-1}/3^k = 1∑k=1∞​2k−1/3k=1. The Cantor set has "length zero".
  • Many points survive: 000, 111, 13\tfrac1331​, 23\tfrac2332​ and every endpoint stay forever. So does 14\tfrac1441​, which is never an endpoint: in base 333, 14=0.020202…3\tfrac14 = 0.020202\ldots_341​=0.020202…3​, since ∑k=1∞2/9k=2/8=1/4\sum_{k=1}^\infty 2/9^k = 2/8 = 1/4∑k=1∞​2/9k=2/8=1/4.
  • Uncountable: x∈Cx \in Cx∈C exactly when xxx has a base-333 expansion using only the digits 000 and 222. Replacing each 222 by 111 and reading the result in base 222 maps CCC onto [0,1][0,1][0,1], so CCC is uncountable.

The Cantor set is the standard example of a set that is "small" in length but "large" in cardinality. It returns in Real Analysis 02 as a closed, compact set that contains no interval.

Practice Exercises

1. Write the negation of: "for every M>0M > 0M>0 there is N∈NN \in \mathbb{N}N∈N such that for all n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N, an>Ma_n > Man​>M" (the definition of an→∞a_n \to \inftyan​→∞).

Solution

"There is M>0M > 0M>0 such that for every N∈NN \in \mathbb{N}N∈N there is n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N with an≤Ma_n \le Man​≤M." In words: there is a level MMM at or below which infinitely many terms stay.

2. Prove by induction that 1+2+⋯+n=n(n+1)21 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}1+2+⋯+n=2n(n+1)​ for all n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N.

Solution

Base: 1=1⋅221 = \frac{1 \cdot 2}{2}1=21⋅2​. Step: if 1+⋯+n=n(n+1)21 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}1+⋯+n=2n(n+1)​, then 1+⋯+n+(n+1)=n(n+1)2+(n+1)=(n+1)(n+2)21 + \cdots + n + (n + 1) = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + (n+1) = \frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}1+⋯+n+(n+1)=2n(n+1)​+(n+1)=2(n+1)(n+2)​, which is the formula for n+1n + 1n+1.

3. Prove that 3\sqrt{3}3​ is irrational.

Solution

First, if 333 divides n2n^2n2 then 333 divides nnn: otherwise n=3k±1n = 3k \pm 1n=3k±1 and n2=9k2±6k+1n^2 = 9k^2 \pm 6k + 1n2=9k2±6k+1 leaves remainder 111 on division by 333. Now suppose 3=p/q\sqrt{3} = p/q3​=p/q in lowest terms. Then p2=3q2p^2 = 3q^2p2=3q2, so 333 divides ppp; write p=3kp = 3kp=3k. Then 9k2=3q29k^2 = 3q^29k2=3q2, so q2=3k2q^2 = 3k^2q2=3k2 and 333 divides qqq. Both divisible by 333 contradicts lowest terms.

4. Find sup⁡A\sup AsupA and inf⁡A\inf AinfA for A={nn+1:n∈N}A = \left\{ \frac{n}{n+1} : n \in \mathbb{N} \right\}A={n+1n​:n∈N} and prove your answer for the supremum.

Solution

inf⁡A=12\inf A = \frac12infA=21​ (the minimum, at n=1n = 1n=1, since nn+1=1−1n+1\frac{n}{n+1} = 1 - \frac{1}{n+1}n+1n​=1−n+11​ increases with nnn). sup⁡A=1\sup A = 1supA=1: it is an upper bound since nn+1<1\frac{n}{n+1} < 1n+1n​<1. Given ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, choose nnn with 1n+1<ε\frac{1}{n+1} < \varepsilonn+11​<ε (Archimedean); then nn+1=1−1n+1>1−ε\frac{n}{n+1} = 1 - \frac{1}{n+1} > 1 - \varepsilonn+1n​=1−n+11​>1−ε. By the ε\varepsilonε-characterization, sup⁡A=1\sup A = 1supA=1. It is not attained.

5. Let A,BA, BA,B be nonempty and bounded above, and A+B={a+b:a∈A,b∈B}A + B = \{a + b : a \in A, b \in B\}A+B={a+b:a∈A,b∈B}. Prove sup⁡(A+B)=sup⁡A+sup⁡B\sup(A + B) = \sup A + \sup Bsup(A+B)=supA+supB.

Solution

Let s=sup⁡As = \sup As=supA, t=sup⁡Bt = \sup Bt=supB. For a∈Aa \in Aa∈A, b∈Bb \in Bb∈B: a+b≤s+ta + b \le s + ta+b≤s+t, so s+ts + ts+t is an upper bound. Given ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, pick a>s−ε/2a > s - \varepsilon/2a>s−ε/2 and b>t−ε/2b > t - \varepsilon/2b>t−ε/2; then a+b>(s+t)−εa + b > (s + t) - \varepsilona+b>(s+t)−ε. By the ε\varepsilonε-characterization, sup⁡(A+B)=s+t\sup(A + B) = s + tsup(A+B)=s+t.

6. Show that the intervals In=(0,1/n]I_n = (0, 1/n]In​=(0,1/n] are nested but have empty intersection. Which hypothesis of the Nested Interval Property fails?

Solution

1/(n+1)<1/n1/(n+1) < 1/n1/(n+1)<1/n gives In+1⊆InI_{n+1} \subseteq I_nIn+1​⊆In​. If x≤0x \le 0x≤0, x∉I1x \notin I_1x∈/I1​. If x>0x > 0x>0, choose nnn with 1/n<x1/n < x1/n<x (Archimedean); then x∉Inx \notin I_nx∈/In​. So the intersection is empty. The intervals are not closed (the left endpoint 000 is missing).

7. Show that the set of all finite subsets of N\mathbb{N}N is countable, but the set P(N)\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})P(N) of all subsets of N\mathbb{N}N is not.

Solution

Finite subsets: for each nnn, the subsets of {1,…,n}\{1, \dots, n\}{1,…,n} form a finite collection (2n2^n2n sets), and every finite subset of N\mathbb{N}N belongs to one of these collections. List the first collection, then the new sets of the second, and so on; this lists every finite subset exactly once. All subsets: suppose f:N→P(N)f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})f:N→P(N) were onto. Let B={n:n∉f(n)}B = \{n : n \notin f(n)\}B={n:n∈/f(n)}. If B=f(m)B = f(m)B=f(m), then m∈B  ⟺  m∉f(m)=Bm \in B \iff m \notin f(m) = Bm∈B⟺m∈/f(m)=B, a contradiction. (This is Cantor's theorem, the same diagonal idea.)

Idea Statement Used for
Negation flip each quantifier, negate the final condition "does not converge", "not continuous"

Reverse triangle ∣∣x∣−∣y∣∣≤∣x−y∣\big\lvert \lvert x\rvert - \lvert y\rvert\big\rvert \le \lvert x - y\rvert​∣x∣−∣y∣​≤∣x−y∣ lower bounds on ∣an∣\lvert a_n \rvert∣an​∣
Equality lemma a=ba = ba=b iff ∣a−b∣<ε\lvert a - b\rvert < \varepsilon∣a−b∣<ε for all ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 proving limits are unique

ε\varepsilonε-test upper bound sss, and some a>s−εa > s - \varepsilona>s−ε for each ε\varepsilonε every sup computation
Completeness nonempty + bounded above gives a sup in R\mathbb{R}R the one axiom Q\mathbb{Q}Q lacks

What's next

Real Analysis 01 uses the Axiom of Completeness to study sequences and series: the ε\varepsilonε–NNN definition of a limit with an explicit NNN, the Monotone Convergence Theorem (a supremum in disguise), Bolzano–Weierstrass (nested intervals in disguise), Cauchy sequences, and the convergence tests for infinite series, including why rearranging a series can change its sum.
